turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Marg, I'll grab a blood pressure before Dr Nguyen comes in. Sleeve up for me, feet on the floor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I only booked for the knee. Is the blood pressure part of that, or have you already found something?
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): It's just routine obs. Try not to talk while it inflates.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Sorry. The waiting room telly was stuck on some renovation show and I couldn't think straight.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): First reading is one seventy-two over one hundred and four. That's high, so I'll repeat it on the other arm.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): One seventy-two? Oh god. My dad had a stroke when he was seventy-one. Am I about to have one in this chair?
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): You're not having a stroke in the chair. Quiet again for the second reading.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I had a flat white on the way in, and the parking meter ate my coins. That'll be why it's up.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Second reading, one fifty-eight over ninety-six. Pulse eighty-four. Still up, just not the same number.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): So which one do you write down? They don't match. I feel awful.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): Both get written down. Two minutes, two readings, both real. Any chest pain right now?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the left knee, from the garden beds. I thought that was the whole appointment.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Chest, love, not the knee. Any pain in the chest?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. No. No chest pain. Sorry, I'm all over the shop.
[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): No worries. I'll let Dr Nguyen know the numbers. He won't be long.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): G'day Marg. Those pressures are on the screen. Before we get stuck into them, what did you actually come in for?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): The left knee. It's been grumbling and I was hoping you'd say it's nothing, so I can keep walking the dog.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long's it been grumbling?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. No, that's wrong. We got back from Lorne three weeks ago and it started the week after, so more like a month.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): A month, then. Which part of the knee, and what sets it off?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Inner side, on the left. Stairs are the worst, and kneeling in the garden. Rest settles it. It's not swollen, I don't think. Should I be icing, and is twenty minutes too long?
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ice in a minute. Any locking, or does it give way?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister reckons I should take magnesium like she does, two tablets every morning for her cramps. Would that help a knee?
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's your sister's magnesium, not yours, and I'm not starting you on it. Locking or giving way — yes or no?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It doesn't lock and it doesn't give way. Just a dull ache.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. Up on the couch and I'll have a feel.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, that spot. Does tender mean a tear? Do I need a scan today? Be honest, I'd rather know.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tender along the medial joint line. No effusion that I can feel, and you bend it fully. I'm not thinking a tear on this.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): So no scan. What if it gets worse next week while I'm looking after my grandson? I do the Thursday school pickup.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. We might get an x-ray if it doesn't settle, but I wouldn't jump to a scan now.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. And Panadol — I've been taking two at night. No, sorry, I take one, five hundred milligrams, just at night if it's aching. Is one enough? Should I take them through the day as well?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): One five-hundred-milligram paracetamol at night is plenty if it takes the edge off. Don't add anything else with paracetamol in it. What about Nurofen?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't take ibuprofen. It played up with my stomach years ago, so I leave it alone. Is that going to matter for the blood pressure?

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): It doesn't change today's plan. First pressure was one seventy-two over one hundred and four, second one fifty-eight over ninety-six, pulse eighty-four. That's the bit I don't want to skate past.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): It's white coat. It always shoots up in here. At home I'm sure it's normal. I've never been on blood pressure tablets. You're not starting me on one today, are you? Dad's stroke has been sitting in my head since she read that first number.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not starting a tablet today. Two readings in a wound-up room don't make the diagnosis, and white coat is a fair thought. What I can't see from here is what it does on your own couch.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not having a stroke this week? Say it plainly. And do I cancel the dog walks, and the garden?

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nothing you've told me sounds like a stroke happening now. You haven't mentioned weakness or headache, and you've already said there's no chest pain. Keep walking the dog if the knee stays a dull ache rather than a sharp one, and ease off the kneeling.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I hadn't said the weakness bit out loud. I haven't had any weakness. No headaches either. I keep jumping ahead of the question, sorry.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright. No weakness and no headache, good. Any diabetes, kidney trouble, or a blood pressure problem already on your file?

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Kidneys are fine as far as I know. Cholesterol was checked last year and they said it was okay, I think. I can't remember the actual number. Do you need it, or is okay enough?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): The number can wait. From what you've said there's no known pressure problem before. Do you smoke, or drink?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. A glass of wine with dinner some nights, not every night. Is the wine doing this? Should I stop tonight, completely?

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't hang today's reading on one glass of wine. Keep it modest while we sort the numbers out. What I want next is a proper home monitor, an upper arm cuff, not a wrist one.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to buy one? The chemist has about six and I won't know which. How many times a day, and do I sit still first? My sister never sits still and her GP has a go at her.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll lend you a clinic cuff from out the front, so no brand decision today. Morning and evening, seated and quiet, two readings each time, for two weeks. Write every single number down.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. What if day one is terrible? Do I come straight in, or ring? I need an actual emergency number or I won't sleep.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): If a reading is over one-eighty on the top number and you've got symptoms — chest pain, weakness, a bad headache — that's hospital, don't wait for me. A high number on its own, no symptoms, ring the clinic the next morning. And don't swallow anyone else's tablets while you wait. Not your sister's magnesium, not your dad's old aspirin.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Dad was on aspirin after the stroke, yes. The bottle's still in the cupboard from when he stayed. I haven't touched it. I wasn't going to.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leave it there. Thinking out loud, if the home readings sit up around the one-fifties or higher, we might start a low-dose blood pressure tablet then, and we might send you for bloods and an ECG before that. Not today, and not on these two numbers alone.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Which tablet? Will it make me dizzy for the school run? And are the bloods fasting? Needles make me go woozy, I should warn you.

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Too early to name a tablet. If we ever get there we'll pick something that doesn't flatten you, and we'll talk about driving then. Bloods wouldn't have to be fasting. The diary comes first.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): And the knee — twenty minutes of ice, is that actually right? Also, do I need a certificate? I told work I might be late back and they're funny about it.

[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Twenty minutes with a tea towel between you and the ice, a few times a day, is plenty. I don't think you need time off. Keep walking, skip the kneeling, Panadol as you've been taking it. If the knee hasn't settled in a month we might x-ray it. Otherwise let it be.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): A month. And you look at the diary before any tablet. Promise me there's no script today.

[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): No script today. Book back in two weeks with the page of readings, and bring the cuff in with you. If the knee is worse rather than just grumbly, come sooner, though I'm not expecting that.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I put the cuff on wrong and the numbers are rubbish? Can the nurse watch me do one so I know I've got it?
[SEG0058] person_1 (NURSE): I'll run through it with you on the way out. Bare arm, arrow over the artery, feet flat, no chatting. Same as we just did.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): And that first number was the frightening one. If I only write down the lower one it looks better. That's cheating, isn't it.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's cheating, yes. Write both. The gap between one seventy-two and one fifty-eight is exactly why I'm not labelling this today.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. White coat, home numbers, no tablets, dog walks stay. I think I've asked the lot. Have I missed something dangerous?
[SEG0062] person_3 (DOCTOR): You've asked plenty. Collect the cuff from the nurse, start tomorrow morning, and we'll go through the page together in a fortnight.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Tomorrow morning. Thanks. Sorry I came in about a knee and turned it into all this.
[SEG0064] person_1 (NURSE): Happens more than you'd think. Come on, I'll show you the machine before you head off.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Patient denies taking ibuprofen now, but transcript doesn't explicitly say it was formally discontinued.

omissions.text: Negative finding omitted: patient denied kidney trouble ('Kidneys are fine as far as I know').
History omitted: patient has never been on blood pressure tablets.
History omitted: cholesterol was checked last year and was said to be okay, though patient could not recall the number.
Medication intolerance detail recorded incompletely: ibuprofen/Nurofen was avoided because it upset her stomach years ago.
Follow-up/plan detail omitted: patient was told to bring the home blood pressure cuff in with her to the two-week review.
